title: The City That Reversed Its River

lines.text: In 1900, Chicago dumped its sewage into the river.
lines.spoken: In nineteen hundred, Chicago dumped its sewage into the river.
lines.hero: the map: the city, the river, the lake

lines.text: And the river ran into the lake it drank from.
lines.spoken: And the river ran straight into the lake it drank from.
lines.hero: the short arrow into the lake

lines.text: So engineers made the river run the other way.
lines.spoken: So engineers made the river run the other way.

lines.text: They cut a canal, twenty eight miles long.
lines.spoken: They cut a canal, twenty eight miles long.
lines.hero: the canal draws from the river west

lines.text: It crossed the low ridge between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi.
lines.spoken: It crossed the low ridge between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi.
lines.hero: the ridge, and the two watersheds

lines.text: Twelve miles west of the lake, that ridge is eight feet high.
lines.spoken: Twelve miles west of the lake, that ridge is only eight feet high.

lines.text: It took eight years, and forty two million cubic yards of rock and clay.
lines.spoken: It took eight years, and forty two million cubic yards of rock and clay.

lines.text: More earth moved than the Panama Canal.
lines.spoken: More earth moved here, than in the Panama Canal.

lines.text: The crews who dug it went on to dig Panama.
lines.spoken: The crews who dug it, went on to dig Panama.

lines.text: On January 2, 1900, at dawn, they broke the last dam at Kedzie Avenue.
lines.spoken: On January second, nineteen hundred, at dawn, they broke the last dam at Kedzie Avenue.

lines.text: Before a court could stop them.
lines.spoken: Before a court could stop them.

lines.text: By the end of the month, the river ran backwards.
lines.spoken: By the end of the month, the river ran backwards.

lines.text: Missouri sued the same month.
lines.spoken: Missouri sued the same month.
lines.hero: MISSOURI fills red on the map

lines.text: The case ran six years, to the Supreme Court.
lines.spoken: The case ran six years, to the Supreme Court.

lines.text: In 1906 the Court ruled for Chicago. It left the question open.
lines.spoken: In nineteen oh six, the Court ruled for Chicago. It left the question open.

lines.text: Holmes wrote that the rivers' fate should not be settled at one blow.
lines.spoken: Holmes wrote that the fate of the rivers should not be settled at one blow.

lines.text: But the downriver towns were right. The canal was too small, and the waste was untreated.
lines.spoken: But the downriver towns were right. The canal was too small, and the waste was untreated.

lines.text: The river still runs backwards.
lines.spoken: The river still runs backwards today.
lines.hero: pull back: the river and the map

lines.text: The canal still carries Chicago's waste.
lines.spoken: The canal still carries Chicago's waste.

lines.text: Electric barriers stand in it now, to keep the Asian carp out of the lake.
lines.spoken: Electric barriers stand in it now, to keep the Asian carp out of the lake.
lines.hero: the barrier mark, on the canal

lines.text: A city solved its problem by moving it three hundred and fifty miles downstream.
lines.spoken: A city solved its problem, by moving it three hundred and fifty miles downstream.

fact_notes: Lake Michigan was Chicago's drinking water and its sewer: sewage went into the river and the river ran into the lake, causing cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Source: WTTW Chicago Stories, 'The Race to Reverse the River'; City Cast Chicago.
The subcontinental divide sits about 12 miles west of the lake shore and the ridge is roughly 8 feet high. Source: Chicago Public Library timeline; WTTW.
Canal: 28 miles, dug 1892-1900, roughly 42 million cubic yards of rock and soil. Source: WTTW; City Cast Chicago; WTTW 'Reversal of the Chicago River'.
More earth moved than the Panama Canal; the methods became the Chicago School of earthmoving and its veterans worked on Panama. Source: Britannica; WTTW; Matt Rickard.

January 2, 1900: Sanitary District trustees went out at dawn to the last earthen dam near Kedzie Avenue and broke it, partly to get ahead of the courts. Source: WTTW; Chicago Daily Tribune via Connecting the Windy City; Chicago Tribune.
The controlling works at Lockport opened January 17, 1900 (the 'end of the month' line is an allowance for that). Source: Connecting the Windy City citing the Tribune; Chicago Public Library.
Missouri filed in the US Supreme Court in January 1900; Missouri v. Illinois decided February 19, 1906, 9-0 for Illinois, Holmes writing. Source: Justia (200 U.S. 496); Ballotpedia.

The canal discharged sewage untreated; treatment plants came only after the 1930 Supreme Court ruling, and downriver complaints that the rivers could not self-purify proved correct. Source: Britannica; We're History; contemporary Supreme Court record.
The reversal persists; the canal is still the Chicago area's outflow, roughly 350 miles from Chicago to the Mississippi (the 1906 record cites 357 miles).

The canal is still the Chicago area's outflow; an electric barrier in the channel is the front line against Asian carp reaching Lake Michigan. Sources: USGS / US Army Corps of Engineers reporting on the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal barrier.
